edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 68 opens on a 3rd-person jussive triad, “Let God arise! Let his enemies be scattered! Let them who hate him also flee before him.” (web:Ps.68.1), followed by the psalm's genuine imperative opener, a four-verb summons, “Sing to God! Sing praises to his name! Extol him who rides on the clouds: to Yah, his name! Rejoice before him!” (web:Ps.68.4). The strophe closes on a verbless construct-noun clause, “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.” (web:Ps.68.5), then the strophe's genuine participles, “God sets the lonely in families. He brings out the prisoners with singing” (web:Ps.68.6); the shift from imperative summons to this closing description marks this strophe's own close before the historical address opens at web:Ps.68.7.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.68.7 to fold in the wilderness-march recollection was rejected: web:Ps.68.7 opens with direct vocative address, “God, when you went out before your people,” a historical-narrative register distinct from the character description of web:Ps.68.5-web:Ps.68.6.
observed_substrate_signals: A 3rd-person jussive triad (“Let… Let… Let…”) opens the psalm (web:Ps.68.1); its verbs are prefix-conjugation forms with expressed subjects, not imperatives.
The psalm's actual imperative opener is a four-verb cluster, “Sing to God! Sing praises…” (web:Ps.68.4), distinct in form from the jussive triad of web:Ps.68.1.

web:Ps.68.5 (“is God in his holy habitation”) is a verbless construct-noun clause, not participial; the strophe's genuine participles open the next verse instead, “God sets the lonely in families. He brings out the prisoners with singing” (web:Ps.68.6), replacing the imperative mood running through web:Ps.68.1 (3rd-person jussive) and web:Ps.68.4 (true imperative).

This composition carries dense fragment-catalog texture and a concentration of hapax and rare forms in its middle third; rows here register medium and medium_low confidence where the byte-verified warrant runs thin, disclosed row by row rather than smoothed over.

edited_rows.rationale: The historical address opens on the wilderness march, “God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness” (web:Ps.68.7), closed by a Selah, and continues through Sinai theophany imagery, “The earth trembled. The sky also poured down rain at the presence of the God of Sinai” (web:Ps.68.8), into a battle report whose vocabulary is genuinely obscure: “She who waits at home divides the plunder” (web:Ps.68.12), “the wings of a dove sheathed with silver, her feathers with shining gold” (web:Ps.68.13), plus “it snowed on Zalmon” (web:Ps.68.14). The strophe is bounded by the vocative-plus-Selah opening at web:Ps.68.7 and the scene shift to direct address of the Bashan mountains at web:Ps.68.15; its interior (web:Ps.68.9-web:Ps.68.14) resists a finer tier-1 split — the identity of the home-waiting figure and the referent of the silver-dove and Zalmon-snow images are argued in the commentary tradition, not settled by the bytes available here.

edited_rows.rationale: A verbless anaphoric description turns to the rival mountain, “The mountains of Bashan are majestic mountains. The mountains of Bashan are rugged.” (web:Ps.68.15), before direct second-person address opens with an envy motif, “Why do you look in envy, you rugged mountains, at the mountain where God chooses to reign?” (web:Ps.68.16). The scene then follows the procession itself: “The chariots of God are tens of thousands and thousands of thousands.” (web:Ps.68.17), tracked “from Sinai, into the sanctuary” (web:Ps.68.17), and “You have ascended on high. You have led away captives.” (web:Ps.68.18). web:Ps.68.15's anaphoric mountain description is a verbless 3rd-person noun chain; the tier-1 vocative-shift opener is the direct address beginning at web:Ps.68.16 (“you rugged mountains”); the chariot count and the referent of “ascended on high” (web:Ps.68.18) are debated across the commentary tradition, holding this strophe at reduced confidence relative to its clearer opening.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Merging web:Ps.68.15-web:Ps.68.18 into the preceding strophe (web:Ps.68.7-web:Ps.68.14) was rejected: the second-person vocative to “you rugged mountains” (web:Ps.68.16) opens a fresh addressee distinct from the third-person historical narration running through web:Ps.68.14.

web:Ps.68.18's “ascended on high” and “led away captives” carry debated referents (triumphal ascent vs. divine enthronement) not settled by the English or MT bytes alone.

edited_rows.rationale: The scene turns to a witnessed temple procession, “They have seen your processions, God, even the processions of my God, my King, into the sanctuary.” (web:Ps.68.24), with singers, minstrels, and tambourine players (web:Ps.68.25) and a congregational acclamation, “Bless God in the congregations, even the Lord in the assembly of Israel!” (web:Ps.68.26) — WEB renders MT's אֱלֹהִ֑ים (oshb:Ps.68.27) as “God” and MT's יְ֝הוָ֗ה as “the Lord” at this one verse, departing from its ordinary “Yahweh” rendering elsewhere in the psalm (e.g. web:Ps.68.20); the substitution is a WEB rendering choice, not a textual variant. A tribal list follows (web:Ps.68.27), then an imperative return, “Your God has commanded your strength. Strengthen, God, that which you have done for us.” (web:Ps.68.28), tribute from Jerusalem's temple (web:Ps.68.29), and a rebuke of “the wild animal of the reeds” (web:Ps.68.30) whose referent (commonly read as an Egypt euphemism) is argued rather than settled by the bytes. The strophe runs as one procession-and-tribute movement between the divine-speech close at web:Ps.68.23 and the closing doxology's imperative opening at web:Ps.68.32.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting this strophe at web:Ps.68.26, isolating the congregational acclamation from the procession description, was considered: the acclamation's imperative “Bless” (oshb:Ps.68.27, Piel 2mp) and its quotation-marked speech frame mark a genuine mood and speech-frame shift from the 3rd-person narration of web:Ps.68.24-web:Ps.68.25. It was rejected because the acclamation still continues the same witnessed-procession scene in content and no second independent tier-1 signal joins it to argue a fresh strophe.

The quoted congregational acclamation at web:Ps.68.26 renders MT's יְ֝הוָ֗ה (oshb:Ps.68.27) as “the Lord” (its own אֱלֹהִ֑ים renders ordinarily as “God”), the psalm's departure from the “Yahweh” rendering used at web:Ps.68.16 and web:Ps.68.20.
An imperative, “Strengthen, God” (web:Ps.68.28), reopens direct address after the tribal list of web:Ps.68.27.

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe opens with the vocative אֱֽלֹהִ֗ים (“God”), then אַתָּ֣ה יָ֭דַעְתָּ, “God, you know my foolishness. My sins aren't hidden from you” (web:Ps.69.5 = oshb:Ps.69.6), a confession that turns into intercession for others not to be shamed through him, addressed to “Lord Yahweh of Armies” and the “God of Israel” (web:Ps.69.6). edited_rows.device_notes: This one row is Psalm 70's entire parent grouping. Psalm 70 stands in a typed doublet relation with Psalm 40's closing plea (web:Ps.40.13-Ps.40.17 = oshb:Ps.40.14-Ps.40.18), a free-standing recension of the same composition. Psalm 40 opens ‘רְצֵ֣ה יְ֭הוָה’ (oshb:Ps.40.14), “Be pleased, Yahweh, to deliver me” (web:Ps.40.13); Psalm 70's own opening reads ‘אֱלֹהִ֥ים…’ (oshb:Ps.70.2), “Hurry, God, to deliver me” (web:Ps.70.1), substituting Elohim for the earlier of Psalm 40's two Yahweh tokens. Both psalms share a matching mid-verse clause (words 8-9 of 11 in each host verse, not verse-final): Psalm 40 reads ‘יִגְדַּ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה’ (oshb:Ps.40.17), “Let Yahweh be exalted!” (web:Ps.40.16); Psalm 70's own reads ‘יִגְדַּ֣ל אֱלֹהִ֑ים’ (oshb:Ps.70.5), “Let God be exalted!” (web:Ps.70.4) — a one-word divine-name substitution in an otherwise matching clause. Both psalms' own actual closes come later — Psalm 40 at web:Ps.40.17 (“Don't delay, my God”), Psalm 70 at web:Ps.70.5 (“Yahweh, don't delay”), as this row's own rationale already states for Psalm 70. This Elohim/Yahweh texture is this row's own legitimate discussion, not a boundary driver, since the psalm is chunked whole; it addresses Psalm 70's own text and makes no claim about which composition is prior.

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 71 carries no title (1 of 34 title-less psalms in the book, per psalm_device_inventory.json) — WEB renders no unnumbered title line for it, and its numbering is identity (WEB verse = MT verse) — so the opening row begins directly at web:Ps.71.1, “In you, Yahweh, I take refuge. Never let me be disappointed.” The imperative cluster that follows — “Deliver me…rescue me…Turn your ear to me, and save me” (web:Ps.71.2) — closes with ‘כִּֽי סַלְעִ֖י וּמְצוּדָתִ֣י אָֽתָּה’ (oshb:Ps.71.3), “for you are my rock and my fortress” (web:Ps.71.3). web:Ps.71.5 shifts to a youth-and-birth retrospective register, closing this opening refuge-and-rescue cluster at web:Ps.71.4's plea to be rescued “from the hand of the wicked”. The refuge root that opens the psalm here, (oshb:Ps.71.1) חָסִ֑יתִי, recurs once more in Psalm 71, (oshb:Ps.71.7) מַֽחֲסִי, inside the following row's span — a bracket straddling this row's own closing seam (web:Ps.71.4|web:Ps.71.5), disclosed here rather than argued as a boundary driver.
